Channel angle: familiar objects with a surprising but true job. Generate five declarative, concrete subject-first hooks; prefer 6-10 words and do not give away the mechanism at once. Six story functions across five voiced scenes of 6 seconds each: visual paradox, contradiction, clue, mechanism, distinct second reveal, payoff. The opening frame shows the object already moving. Start the mechanism about 5 seconds in, at the clue scene. Loop: scene 5 (payoff) must end on the same object and the same framing as the first frame of scene 1 so the Short loops seamlessly. YouTube title seed: What Are Those Giant Balls on Power Lines For?
YouTube description seed: Those balls on power lines have a job most people never guess. What did you think they were for? Sources: US FAA obstruction marking standard AC 70/7460-1N. #TellMeWhyyyyyy #Shorts
The central fact: In the US, marker balls make overhead wires easy for pilots to spot from far away.
The later surprise: Their colors alternate because mixing orange, white and yellow stands out best against any background.
The very first frame shows a pilot's-eye view from a moving light aircraft over a river valley, where a power line is nearly invisible against the land until orange, white and yellow marker balls suddenly pop into view on the top wire. Already moving in the first frame; do not reveal the mechanism in the opening.
What changes inside each 6s clip:
Scene 1 (contradiction, 0-6s): Opening: pilot's-eye view in motion, with the wire nearly invisible. About 2s in, the marker balls suddenly pop into view. About 4s in, the aircraft climbs, keeping the balls in frame.
Scene 2 (clue, 6-12s): Mechanism starts about 5s in. Ground view of one ball swaying, then framing tightens onto the thin cable, which nearly vanishes against the sky. About 2-3s later, a distant hillside view where only the balls stay visible, then a reframing toward a big ball on a long span over the river.
Scene 3 (mechanism, 12-18s): Pilot-eye view from a moving light aircraft approaching the line; about 2s in the balls become clear first; about 4s in the plane climbs over the line.
Scene 4 (second_reveal, 18-24s): Slow lateral move along a long span showing alternating orange, white and yellow balls; about every 2s the background changes (sky, trees, hills) and a different color stands out.
Scene 5 (payoff, 24-30s): Lines near a runway end with closer spacing; about 3s in, return to the exact opening: the same pilot's-eye view over the same river valley with the nearly invisible wire and the balls popping into view, same framing as scene 1's first frame, so it loops.
Fact boundaries: US standard only; other countries may differ. Not every power line has markers; they are mainly used on lines under 69 kV and in spots that are hard for pilots to see. Do not claim exact sizes beyond the 36-inch and 20-inch markers the source names.

facts.statement: In the US, marker balls make overhead wires easy for pilots to spot, and they should be visible in clear daylight from at least 4,000 feet away.
The balls alternate solid orange, white and yellow because mixing colors stands out best against every background, and the ends of a line normally get orange.
The balls are spaced about every 200 feet, and closer together near runway ends.
On long wires that cross canyons, lakes and rivers, the balls should be at least 36 inches across, nearly a meter.
